questions.sec: Parietal map, postcentral gyrus and motor-fibre origins
questions.q: The Praxicons page places the parietal lobe in which relation to the central sulcus, and labels primary sensory cortex as which areas?
opts: Medial to the corpus callosum; areas 9, 10 and 11
Posterior to the central sulcus; areas 3, 1 and 2
Anterior to the central sulcus; areas 4, 6 and 8
Inferior to the Sylvian fissure; areas 17 and 18
questions.exp: The page heading says parietal lobe posterior to the central sulcus and labels primary sensory cortex as areas 3, 1 and 2. (Book p560)

questions.sec: Parietal map, postcentral gyrus and motor-fibre origins
questions.q: Which set of landmarks belongs to the posterior-parietal diagram?
opts: Rectus gyrus, olfactory sulcus, orbital sulcus and orbital gyri
Hippocampal gyrus, uncus, fornix and cingulate sulcus only
Posterior parietal lobule, intraparietal sulcus, superior and inferior parietal lobules, supramarginal gyrus, angular gyrus and parieto-occipital association area
Precentral gyrus, premotor area, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.exp: The parietal map labels the posterior parietal lobule and intraparietal sulcus, superior parietal lobule as praxicons, inferior parietal lobule, supramarginal gyrus as gnosis, angular gyrus as Gerstmann syndrome and the parieto-occipital association area. (Book p560)

questions.sec: Parietal map, postcentral gyrus and motor-fibre origins
questions.q: What proportions of motor fibres are assigned to the three cortical sources in the note?
opts: Primary sensory 10%, primary motor 80%, premotor plus supplementary 10%
Primary sensory 30%, primary motor 30%, premotor plus supplementary 40%
Primary sensory 50%, primary motor 25%, premotor plus supplementary 25%
Primary sensory cortex 40%, primary motor cortex 30%, and premotor plus supplementary motor cortex 30%
questions.exp: The origin-of-motor-fibres note gives primary sensory cortex 40%, primary motor cortex 30% and premotor/supplementary motor cortex 30%. (Book p560)

questions.sec: Parietal map, postcentral gyrus and motor-fibre origins
questions.q: A postcentral-gyrus lesion is described as causing contralateral UMN weakness with the page's vascular association. Which vessel is named?
opts: Middle cerebral artery
Anterior cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery
Basilar artery
questions.exp: Under postcentral gyrus, contralateral upper-motor-neuron weakness is associated with the middle cerebral artery. (Book p560)

questions.sec: Parietal map, postcentral gyrus and motor-fibre origins
questions.q: Compared with a primary motor-cortex lesion, the postcentral-gyrus profile on the page includes which combination?
opts: Tone is unchanged, the FEF is affected and only language is impaired
Tone is less affected, the frontal eye field is spared and cortical sensations are impaired
Tone is severely increased, the FEF is destroyed and cortical sensations are normal
Tone is flaccid, the FEF is spared and only hearing is impaired
questions.exp: The postcentral-gyrus list states that tone is less affected, the frontal eye field is spared and cortical sensations are impaired. (Book p560)

questions.sec: Parietal map, postcentral gyrus and motor-fibre origins
questions.q: Which group is explicitly listed under impaired cortical sensations?
opts: Smell, hearing, taste and visual acuity
Fluency, insight, judgement and abstract thinking
Tactile localisation, two-point discrimination, stereognosis and graphesthesia
Pain, temperature, vibration and joint position only
questions.exp: The page lists impaired cortical sensations as tactile localisation, two-point discrimination, stereognosis and graphesthesia. (Book p560)

questions.sec: Parietal map, postcentral gyrus and motor-fibre origins
questions.q: What association and blood-supply notes accompany the postcentral-gyrus section?
opts: Association with the cerebellum relates to smell; primary cortices are supplied by PCA
Association with the hippocampus relates to memory; primary cortices are supplied by ACA only
Association with Broca area relates to hearing; primary cortices have no named arterial supply
Association with premotor and supplementary motor areas relates to tone and FEF; primary sensory and primary motor cortices are supplied by MCA
questions.exp: The notes link premotor/supplementary motor association with tone and FEF, and state that primary sensory and primary motor cortices have middle-cerebral-artery blood supply. (Book p560)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: What does the superior parietal lobule generate according to the page?
opts: Praxicons: a movement formula and sensory guidance for movement
A visual field defect and a motor speech programme
Only the emotional intonation of language
The basal-ganglia neurotransmitter loop
questions.exp: The superior parietal lobule is stated to generate praxicons, defined here as the movement formula or sensory guidance for movement. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: A patient cannot execute a learned voluntary skilled action despite normal cerebellar, motor and sensory function and preserved comprehension. What syndrome is described?
opts: Aphasia from a dominant frontal lesion
Apraxia
Ataxia from a cerebellar lesion
A lower-motor-neuron palsy
questions.exp: Apraxia is defined as inability to execute a learnt voluntary skilled action despite normal cerebellum, motor and sensory function and comprehension. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: What does a superior-parietal-lobule lesion do in the printed model?
opts: It causes isolated lower-limb urinary incontinence
It causes a homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
It causes inability to generate praxicons
It causes inability to recognise an object by touch only
questions.exp: The page directly states that a lesion in the superior parietal lobule causes inability to generate praxicons. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: A patient has lost the idea of a learned skilled act itself. Which apraxia type fits the page?
opts: Ideomotor apraxia
Constructional apraxia
Dressing apraxia
Ideational apraxia
questions.exp: Ideational apraxia is printed as the type in which the idea is absent. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: A patient understands the idea of a skilled action but executes it poorly. Which apraxia type is this?
opts: Ideomotor apraxia
Ideational apraxia
Topographic agnosia
Hemispatial neglect
questions.exp: Ideomotor apraxia is printed as idea present with poor execution. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: What does gnosis mean in the supramarginal-gyrus section?
opts: The ability to generate a movement formula from the cerebellum
The ability to recognise an object by touch, vision or sound
The inability to execute a learned action despite normal comprehension
The inability to differentiate a bedroom from a bathroom
questions.exp: Gnosis is defined as the ability to recognise an object by touch, vision or sound. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: A patient cannot identify an object by vision, with the page's affected areas being considered. Which finding is being described?
opts: Pure alexia involving the fusiform gyrus only
A frontal eye-field lesion involving the PPRF
Visual agnosia involving the supramarginal gyrus and parieto-occipital association area for visuospatial orientation
Ideational apraxia involving the superior parietal lobule only
questions.exp: Visual agnosia is described as inability to identify by vision; the page names the supramarginal gyrus and the parieto-occipital association area, the latter linked to visuospatial orientation. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: For the dominant parietal lobe table, which handedness percentages are printed?
opts: Right-handed: right 90–95% and left 5%; left-handed: right 50–60% and left 40%
Right-handed: both lobes 50%; left-handed: both lobes 50%
Right-handed: right 40% and left 50–60%; left-handed: right 5% and left 90–95%
Right-handed: right lobe 5% and left lobe 90–95%; left-handed: right lobe 40% and left lobe 50–60%
questions.exp: The table prints right-handed dominance as right lobe 5% and left lobe 90–95%, and left-handed dominance as right lobe 40% and left lobe 50–60%. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: The page places language in which relationship to the dominant parietal lobe?
opts: Language is part of the dominant lobe
Language is restricted to the non-dominant lobe
Language is part of the cerebellum rather than either parietal lobe
Language is assigned only to the occipital lobe
questions.exp: Immediately below the dominance table, the source states that language is part of the dominant lobe. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: Which non-dominant-parietal pattern is correctly interpreted as pseudoapraxia?
opts: Both are defined as loss of the idea of a skilled action from a dominant superior parietal lesion
Constructional apraxia is inability to perceive and imagine geometric relations, while dressing apraxia is inability to dress, such as being unable to put on a jacket
Constructional apraxia is inability to read, while dressing apraxia is inability to name fingers
Constructional apraxia is inability to recognise by sound, while dressing apraxia is loss of bladder control
questions.exp: The non-dominant parietal section calls these pseudoapraxias: constructional apraxia is inability to perceive and imagine geometric relation, and dressing apraxia is inability to dress, exemplified by inability to put on a jacket. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
questions.q: A patient cannot distinguish familiar places such as the bedroom and bathroom. Which non-dominant-parietal deficit is printed?
opts: Graphesthesia
Ideomotor apraxia
Visuospatial disorientation
Anomia
questions.exp: Visuospatial disorientation is defined as inability to differentiate places, for example bedroom and bathroom. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
questions.q: A patient visually scans only one side of the body schema and neglects activities related to one hemisphere. Which syndrome is named?
opts: Topographic agnosia
Ideomotor apraxia
Pure alexia without agraphia
Hemispatial neglect, also termed anosognosia/asomatognosia in the note
questions.exp: The page introduces hemispatial neglect with anosognosia/asomatognosia as abnormal visual scanning of the body schema leading to neglect of activities related to one hemisphere. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
questions.q: Which right-versus-left parietal lesion pairing is printed in the extrapersonal-space table?
opts: Right parietal lesion: left hemispatial neglect; left parietal lesion: no abnormality
Right parietal lesion: no abnormality; left parietal lesion: bilateral neglect
Right parietal lesion: right neglect; left parietal lesion: left neglect
Both right and left parietal lesions cause only right hemispatial neglect
questions.exp: The table shows extrapersonal space represented as right plus left under the right parietal lobe and right under the left parietal lobe; a right-parietal lesion gives left hemispatial neglect, while the left-parietal lesion column says no abnormality. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
questions.q: What is topographic agnosia?
opts: Loss of a visual field with preserved spatial orientation
Loss of orientation to topography
Loss of the idea of a learned motor act
Loss of reading with preserved writing
questions.exp: Topographic agnosia is defined on the page as loss of orientation to topography. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
questions.q: Which function set is assigned to the angular gyrus?
opts: Eye abduction, adduction and the vestibulo-ocular reflex
Pain, temperature, vibration and primary touch only
Reading, writing, naming and spatial orientation with respect to fingers, numbers and body sites
Postural tone, proximal alignment and antagonist inhibition
questions.exp: The angular-gyrus functions listed are reading, writing, naming and spatial orientation with respect to finger, number and body sites. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
questions.q: A dominant angular-gyrus lesion produces impaired reading and writing, impaired naming, finger anomia, acalculia and right-left disorientation. Which syndrome is this?
opts: Horner syndrome
Brown-Sequard syndrome
Wernicke syndrome
Gerstmann syndrome
questions.exp: Gerstmann syndrome is attributed to a lesion of the dominant angular gyrus and includes alexia plus agraphia, anomia, finger anomia or acalculia, and right-to-left disorientation. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
questions.q: Which pairing correctly expands the two reading/writing deficits in Gerstmann syndrome?
opts: Alexia means impaired reading and agraphia means impaired writing
Alexia means impaired writing and agraphia means impaired reading
Alexia means impaired naming and agraphia means impaired calculation
Alexia means impaired touch recognition and agraphia means impaired vision
questions.exp: The Gerstmann list explicitly pairs alexia with impaired reading and agraphia with impaired writing. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
questions.q: A left PCA infarct involving the splenium is followed by an occipital lesion with normal vision because of macular sparing, a right homonymous hemianopia and loss of connection between cortices. Which additional disconnection finding is printed?
opts: Fluent aphasia with preserved naming
Alexia without agraphia
Agraphia without alexia
Bilateral deafness with preserved reading
questions.exp: The note links left PCA infarct plus splenium of corpus callosum to an occipital lesion with macular sparing, right homonymous hemianopia and a disconnection syndrome, including alexia without agraphia. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
questions.q: Where does the page localise pure alexia?
opts: A lesion of the precentral gyrus
A lesion of the PPRF
A lesion of the fusiform gyrus
A lesion of the superior parietal lobule
questions.exp: The visual-abnormalities note states that pure alexia is due to a fusiform-gyrus lesion. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
questions.q: Which lobe-to-visual-field pattern is transcribed in the final list?
opts: Frontal lobe—ipsilateral hemianopia; parietal lobe—superior quadrantanopia; temporal lobe—inferior quadrantanopia
Frontal lobe—bitemporal hemianopia; parietal lobe—central scotoma; temporal lobe—monocular blindness
All three lobes produce only macular sparing with no quadrantanopia
Frontal lobe—contralateral hemianopia; parietal lobe—inferior homonymous quadrantanopia or pie in the floor; temporal lobe—superior homonymous quadrantanopia or pie in the sky
questions.exp: The final visual list assigns contralateral hemianopia to frontal lobe, inferior homonymous quadrantanopia or pie in the floor to parietal lobe, and superior homonymous quadrantanopia or pie in the sky to temporal lobe. (Book p562)

units.title: 1. Parietal map, postcentral gyrus and motor-fibre origins
units.sec: Parietal map, postcentral gyrus and motor-fibre origins
units.guide:
The posterior-central-sulcus map identifies primary sensory cortex and the parietal association regions.
The motor-fibre percentages and the postcentral-gyrus lesion profile retain the page's supplied MCA, tone, FEF and cortical-sensation notes.

units.title: 2. Praxicons, apraxias and parietal dominance
units.guide:
The superior parietal lobule generates the movement formula and sensory guidance for movement.
Apraxia, visual agnosia, handedness-based dominant-parietal percentages and non-dominant pseudoapraxias are kept in the printed order.

units.title: 3. Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
units.sec: Hemispatial neglect, angular gyrus and visual pathways
units.guide:
Right-versus-left parietal neglect, topographic agnosia, angular-gyrus functions and Gerstmann syndrome are followed by the PCA/splenium note.
Pure alexia and the frontal, parietal and temporal visual-field patterns close the source range at Book p562.
